title: What Virginia’s New Data Center Executive Order Means for Developers and How Bowman Can Help You Stay Ahead of It
summary: Virginia’s new data center framework changes local approval, water, noise and power planning. See what developers need to know and how Bowman can help.
body_markdown:
With more data center capacity than any other state, Virginia is where the industry’s next standards are taking shape. On September 18, 2026, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger signed[Executive Order 22 (EO 22)](https://www.governor.virginia.gov/media/governorvirginiagov/governor-of-virginia/pdf/eo/eo-22-establishing-va-data-center-accountability-and-ai-initiatives.pdf) , creating the[Virginia Data Center Accountability Framework](https://www.governor.virginia.gov/media/governorvirginiagov/governor-of-virginia/pdf/Data-Center-Accountability-Framework.pdf) . Under the new framework, Virginia data centers will soon face a higher bar for how they’re built, sited and operated, and similar expectations may spread beyond the Commonwealth.


For developers, operators and hyperscalers active in Virginia or weighing it for future facilities, the framework acts like a roadmap. The Governor is moving many of its directives through EO 22 now and plans to work with the General Assembly to write the standards into law in the 2027 session. Projects that understand what’s coming and act early are better positioned to clear approval.


Here’s what the framework asks for and what it means in practice.


## **What the Framework Requires**


The framework is built around[five goals](https://www.governor.virginia.gov/media/governorvirginiagov/governor-of-virginia/pdf/Data-Center-Accountability-Framework.pdf) : **increased transparency** , **environmental protection** , **ratepayer affordability,** **clean energy and grid reliability** and **workforce benefits** . EO 22 puts many of its directives in motion now, starting with a Data Center Planning and Community Engagement Toolkit due within 120 days, with model disclosure templates for project impacts such as electricity demand, water use, noise and traffic.


Beyond the Toolkit, EO 22 takes several immediate actions, including


*Expand the sections below for a breakdown of each framework.*


###


Expect more disclosure, more local control and fewer state shortcuts. The framework calls for:


- A ban on nondisclosure agreements that keep communities uninformed about planned development
- An end to by-right approval, with local approval required for any data center using more than 25 MW, regardless of prior approvals
- Removal of future large projects from state fast-track permitting, plus an end to state subsidies in site development programs
- Community benefits agreements between operators and local communities, with state resources to help communities negotiate them
- Establishing the Virginia Local Energy and Accountable Data Centers (VA-LEAD) designation standards that recognize data centers exceeding requirements on clean energy, water stewardship, grid support and community benefits
- Promoting projects that protect historic and cultural resources and improve neighborhoods through design, landscaping and buffers


###


Data center projects in Virginia must now meet higher standards on emissions, water stewardship, noise, land use and cumulative community impact. The framework calls for:


- Establishing nation-leading standards for energy efficiency, water use, land impacts and backup generation, including clear water-use standards that cut overall consumption, backed by stronger state enforcement
- Expedited state regulations on data center noise and on cooling water scarcity areas
- Cumulative impact analysis of diesel backup generators, with existing and future facilities moving to cleaner backup power, Tier IV or better
- Encouragement for water-positive developments that replenish local watersheds, plus water reuse and waste heat recovery with nearby businesses and industries
- Priority for brownfields and edge facilities, plus low-impact site design that minimizes land disturbance, reduces the impact of impervious surfaces and maximizes tree cover
- Options for reducing and mitigating impacts on scenic and historic landscapes, including those from transmission lines, plus strategies for end-of-life decommissioning


###


Expect to carry more of the grid costs your project creates, and to show financial commitment earlier. The framework calls for:


- Requiring utilities to allocate a more equitable share of transmission and generation costs to data centers and other large load customers
- Requiring stronger upfront financial commitments from developers, so speculative projects do not tie up land, resources and energy infrastructure without ever getting built
- Advocating fair cost allocation with PJM Interconnection, including by working with other states in PJM territory and adding state protections where needed


###


Data centers are expected to work alongside utilities to support new clean generation, energy efficiency and flexible demand, and to strengthen grid resilience and reliability. The framework calls for:


- Limits on electricity generated from on-site natural gas to the maximum extent practicable, and closing loopholes that let those emissions bypass Virginia’s clean air standards and avoid payments into the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative
- Priority grid access for data centers that source clean energy five years faster than the Virginia Clean Economy Act requires, cut backup generator emissions by 60% and allow at most a de minimis amount of on-site natural gas generation, with a doubled electricity consumption tax for operators that then fail to comply
- Easier paths to bring your own clean power, including reforming utility charges that discourage clean energy investment and procurement
- Standards that prevent sudden changes in electricity demand from destabilizing the grid
- Greater flexibility from new and existing data centers to support grid reliability, including through local clean energy and battery projects
- A strategy to prevent and reduce methane emissions across the supply chain and support verified low-emissions gas


###


Virginia wants data center growth to produce quality local jobs, training opportunities and prioritize local procurement. The framework calls for:


- Prioritizing local hiring and encouraging localities to set hiring and workforce training goals
- Prioritizing Virginia businesses in procurement and contracting
- Supporting strong labor practices through responsible contractor standards and apprenticeship programs for new developments
- Supporting project labor agreements where possible


## **Planning Your Data Center Project Around the Framework**


None of this is a reason to pause data center development plans in Virginia, but it does change what “shovel-ready” looks like. Projects with strong water stewardship, credible noise mitigation, a clean backup power strategy and a well-prepared local entitlement case will hold advantage as these standards take effect. Conversely, projects still planning around the assumption of state fast-track eligibility or older diesel backup generation should revisit those assumptions now.


The good news is that most of what the farmwork asks for is established engineering practice. That includes site selection and entitlement strategy, noise and acoustic studies, water resource planning, battery storage and clean backup power design and adaptive reuse of existing buildings. Development teams that bring these capabilities together on one project team will move fastest.
